46added-- HIDE: This file and all later ones should make a habit of always
47added-- presenting both syntax and semantics of new language constructs in
48added-- informal style as well as formal. See MoreStlc.v for a template.
49added
50added-- In the final chaper of *Logical Foundations* (*Software Foundations*,
51added-- volume 1), we began applying the mathematical tools developed in the first
52added-- part of the course to studying the theory of a small programming language,
53added-- Imp.
54added
55added-- - We defined a type of *abstract syntax trees* for Imp, together with an
56added-- *evaluation relation* (a partial function on states) that specifies the
57added-- *operational semantics* of programs.
58added
59added-- The language we defined, though small, captures some of the key features of
60added-- full-blown languages like C, C++, and Java, including the fundamental
61added-- notion of mutable state and some common control structures.
62added
63added-- - We proved a number of *metatheoretic properties* -- "meta" in the sense
64added-- that they are properties of the language as a whole, rather than of
65added-- particular programs in the language. These included:
66added
67added-- - determinism of evaluation
68added
69added-- - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the definitions (e.g.,
70added-- functional and relational definitions of arithmetic expression evaluation)
71added
72added-- - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
73added
74added-- - correctness (in the sense of preserving meaning) of a number of useful
75added-- program transformations
76added
77added-- - behavioral equivalence of programs (in the *Equiv* chapter).
78added
79added-- If we stopped here, we would already have something useful: a set of tools
80added-- for defining and discussing programming languages and language features
81added-- that are mathematically precise, flexible, and easy to work with, applied
82added-- to a set of key properties. All of these properties are things that
83added-- language designers, compiler writers, and users might care about knowing.
84added-- Indeed, many of them are so fundamental to our understanding of the
85added-- programming languages we deal with that we might not consciously recognize
86added-- them as "theorems." But properties that seem intuitively obvious can
87added-- sometimes be quite subtle (sometimes also subtly wrong!).
88added
89added-- We'll return to the theme of metatheoretic properties of whole languages
90added-- later in this volume when we discuss *types* and *type soundness*. In this
91added-- chapter, though, we turn to a different set of issues.
92added
93added-- Our goal in this chapter is to develop the tools to work through some
94added-- simple examples of *program verification* -- i.e., to use the precise
95added-- definition of Imp to prove formally that particular programs satisfy
96added-- particular specifications of their behavior.
97added
98added-- We'll develop a reasoning system called *Floyd-Hoare Logic* -- often
99added-- shortened to just *Hoare Logic* -- in which each of the syntactic
100added-- constructs of Imp is equipped with a generic "proof rule" that can be used
101added-- to reason compositionally about the correctness of programs involving this
102added-- construct.
103added
104added-- Hoare Logic originated in the 1960s, and it continues to be the subject of
105added-- intensive research right up to the present day. It lies at the core of a
106added-- multitude of tools that are being used in academia and industry to specify
107added-- and verify real software systems.
108added
109added-- Hoare Logic combines two beautiful ideas: a natural way of writing down
110added-- *specifications* of programs, and a *structured proof technique* for
111added-- proving that programs are correct with respect to such specifications --
112added-- where by "structured" we mean that the structure of proofs directly mirrors
113added-- the structure of the programs that they are about.
114added
115added-- Note to developers:
116added-- `HIDE: MRC'20: The terse version used to start with just an outline of
117added-- what we've done and of this chapter, but it never mentioned Hoare logic!
118added-- The text above seems like a better intro.
119added--
120added-- MRC'20: this is the former terse intro.
121added--
122added-- What we've done so far:
123added--
124added-- - Formalized Imp
125added-- - identifiers and states
126added-- - abstract syntax trees
127added-- - evaluation functions (for [aexp]s and [bexp]s)
128added-- - evaluation relation (for commands)
129added--
130added-- - Proved some _metatheoretic_ properties
131added-- - determinism of evaluation
132added-- - equivalence of some different ways of writing down the
133added-- definitions (e.g., functional and relational definitions of
134added-- arithmetic expression evaluation)
135added-- - guaranteed termination of certain classes of programs
136added-- - meaning-preservation of some program transformations
137added-- - behavioral equivalence of programs ([Equiv])
138added--
139added-- We've dealt with a few sorts of properties of Imp programs:
140added-- - Termination
141added-- - Nontermination
142added-- - Equivalence
143added--
144added-- Topic:
145added-- - A systematic method for reasoning about the _functional
146added-- correctness_ of programs in Imp
147added--
148added-- Goals:
149added-- - a natural notation for _program specifications_ and
150added-- - a _compositional_ proof technique for program correctness
151added--
152added-- Plan:
153added-- - specifications (assertions / Hoare triples)
154added-- - proof rules
155added-- - loop invariants
156added-- - decorated programs
157added-- - examples`
158added
159added-- ## Assertions
160added
161added-- An *assertion* is a logical claim about the state of a program's memory --
162added-- formally, a property of `State`s.
163added
164addedabbrev Assertion := State → Prop
165added
166added-- Note to developers:
167added-- HIDE: MRC'20: pulled up these examples from the quiz/optional exercise
168added-- so that there would be some modeling of the kinds of answers we expect.
169added
170added-- For example,
171added
172added-- - `fun st => st[X] = 3` holds for states `st` in which value of `X` is `3`,
173added-- - `fun st => True` hold for all states, and
174added-- - `fun st => False` holds for no states.
175added
176added-- _Quiz:_
177added
178added-- Paraphrase the following assertions in English (i.e., say which states
179added-- satisfy them)
180added
181added-- (A) `fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
182added
183added-- (B) `fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]`
184added
185added-- (C)
186added-- `fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧ ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])`
187added
188added-- ### Exercise (1 star): assertions ⭐
189added
190added-- Paraphrase the following assertions in English (or your favorite natural
191added-- language).
192added
193addednamespace ExAssertions
194addeddef assertion1 : Assertion := fun st => st[X] ≤ st[Y]
195addeddef assertion2 : Assertion :=
196added fun st => st[X] = 3 ∨ st[X] ≤ st[Y]
197addeddef assertion3 : Assertion :=
198added fun st => st[Z] * st[Z] ≤ st[X] ∧
199added ¬ ((st[Z] + 1) * (st[Z] + 1) ≤ st[X])
200addeddef assertion4 : Assertion :=
201added fun st => st[Z] = max st[X] st[Y]
202added
203added-- 1. The value of X is less or equal than the value of Y.
204added-- 2. The value of X is 3 or is less or equal than the value of Y.
205added-- 3. The value of Z is the integer square root of X.
206added-- 4. The value of Z is the greater of the values of X and Y
207added
208addedend ExAssertions
209added
210added-- ### Notations for Assertions
211added
212added-- This way of writing assertions can be a little bit heavy, for two reasons:
213added-- (1) every single assertion that we ever write is going to begin with
214added-- `fun st => `; and (2) this state `st` is the only one that we ever use to
215added-- look up variables in assertions (we will almost never need to talk about
216added-- two different memory states at the same time). For discussing examples
217added-- informally, we'll adopt some simplifying conventions: we'll drop the
218added-- initial `fun st =>`, and we'll write just `X` to mean `st[X]`. Thus,
219added-- instead of writing
220added
221added-- fun st => st[X] = m
222added
223added-- we'll write just
224added
225added-- {{ X = m }}.
226added
227added-- Here the "doubly curly" braces `{{` and `}}` delimit the scope of an
228added-- assertion. We'll see more examples below.
229added
230added-- This example also illustrates a convention that we'll use throughout the
231added-- Hoare Logic chapters: in informal assertions, capital letters like `X`,
232added-- `Y`, and `Z` are Imp variables, while lowercase letters like `x`, `y`, `m`,
233added-- and `n` are ordinary Lean variables (of type `Nat`). This is why, when
234added-- translating from informal to formal, we replace `X` with `st[X]` but leave
235added-- `m` alone.
236added

245added-- Note to developers:
246added-- `HIDE: SAZ 2024: I'm confused by the above discussion. Doesn't
247added-- [Add Printing Coercion Aexp_of_nat Aexp_of_aexp assert_of_Prop]

249added--
250added-- `HIDE: SAZ 2024:
251added-- From what I can tell, the reason the notations expand during
252added-- the proofs is that they're writen in such a way that they
253added-- inlude type annotations [(a : Aexp)] and explicit lambdas
254added-- [(fun st => a st + b st)], neither of which is stable under
255added-- simplification. For example:
256added--
257added-- [(fun st =>
258added-- (fun st => (X:Aexp) st + (Y:Aexp) st) st +
259added-- (fun st => (Z:Aexp) st) st)]
260added--
261added-- Will print as [X + Y + Z] until simplification, at which point
262added-- we have [(fun st => st X + st Y + st Z)] but there is no notation
263added-- that covers this case.`
264added
265added-- The convention described above can be implemented with a little syntax
266added-- magic, using coercions and a custom grammar, much as we did with the
267added-- `imp { … }` notation in Imp. This new notation automatically lifts `Aexp`s,
268added-- numbers, and `Prop`s into `Assertion`s when they appear between the
269added-- `{{ _ }}` brackets, or when Lean knows that the type of an expression is
270added-- `Assertion`.
271added
272added-- There is no need to understand the details of how these notation hacks
273added-- work. (We barely understand some of it ourselves!)
274added
275added-- Note to developers:
276added-- HIDE: Assertion-level arith expressions. (BCP: Not sure this is an
277added-- optimally clear name.)
278added--
279added-- One An (meluge): the Rocq development calls this type `Aexp`, in
280added-- contrast to the object-level `aexp`. In Lean the object-level syntax
281added-- type is named `Aexp` in Imp, so we use `Aexp'` for the assertion level
282added-- version.
283added
284addedabbrev Aexp' : Type := State → Nat
285added
286added-- Note to developers:
287added-- HIDE: Some coercions
288added
289addeddef Assertion.ofProp (P : Prop) : Assertion := fun _ => P
290addeddef Aexp'.ofNat (n : Nat) : Aexp' := fun _ => n
291added
292added-- Note to developers:
293added-- HIDE: maybe this one should be explicit.
294added
295addeddef Aexp'.ofAexp (a : Aexp) : Aexp' := fun st => a.eval st
296added
297added@[simp] theorem Assertion.ofProp_apply (P : Prop) (st : State) :
298added Assertion.ofProp P st = P := rfl
299added@[simp] theorem Aexp'.ofNat_apply (n : Nat) (st : State) :
300added Aexp'.ofNat n st = n := rfl
301added@[simp] theorem Aexp'.ofAexp_apply (a : Aexp) (st : State) :
302added Aexp'.ofAexp a st = a.eval st := rfl
303added
304addedinstance : Coe Prop Assertion := ⟨Assertion.ofProp⟩
305addedinstance : Coe Nat Aexp' := ⟨Aexp'.ofNat⟩
306addedinstance (n : Nat) : OfNat Aexp' n := ⟨Aexp'.ofNat n⟩
307addedinstance : Coe Aexp Aexp' := ⟨Aexp'.ofAexp⟩
308addedinstance : Coe Ident Aexp' := ⟨fun x => Aexp'.ofAexp (.id x)⟩

311added-- HIDE: Make things easily unfoldable.

333added-- Note to developers:
334added-- NOTATION: BCP 20: It probably makes sense now to put all these in a
335added-- custom grammar, so that we can really control how it looks and get rid
336added-- of things like ap.
337added--
338added-- `NOTATION: SAZ 2024: I have tried to implement the suggestion above.
339added--
340added-- There is now a custom entry [assn] for defining the syntax of
341added-- assertions. Like the delimiters <{ }> used for Imp programs,
342added-- we now also have {{ }} delimiters for use with Assertions.
343added--
344added-- Inside that scope, the meaning of variables, nat literals,
345added-- propositions, etc. is "lifted" to take a state parameter.
346added--
347added-- The notation {{ #f x1 .. xn }} now "lifts" a normal function
348added-- that should be of type [nat -> .. -> nat -> T] so that each of
349added-- the inputs is treated as an [Aexp] and the state is threaded through.
350added-- (This replaces the need for [ap], [ap2], etc. throughout.)
351added--
352added-- The notation {{ $rocq_term }} now "quotes" a rocq term literally
353added-- without lifting. Parentheses can be used as in {{ $(foo bar) }}.`
354added
355added-- Note to developers (Claude):
356added-- Delaborators for this grammar are defined in the *Printing Assertions*
357added-- section below (after assertion substitution, the last notation they
358added-- need to recognize). They cover the base chapter's forms -- triples,
359added-- `->>`, substitution, and lifted `Prop`s; not covered are the extension
360added-- modules' shadowed triples (each module defines its own `Com` and
361added-- `ValidHoareTriple`) and the `bassertion` coercion, which fall back to
362added-- raw display. An assertion applied to a state (after `intro st`) also
363added-- prints raw -- the same thing that happens in the Rocq development as
364added-- soon as `simpl` unfolds the notation.
365added
366added/-- Assertion-level arithmetic expressions -/
367addeddeclare_syntax_cat assn_aexp
368added/-- Numeric literal -/
369addedsyntax:max num : assn_aexp
370added/-- A variable: an Imp variable, or a Lean identifier of type `Nat`,
371added`Aexp`, or `Aexp'` -/
372addedsyntax:max ident : assn_aexp
373added/-- Lifted application of a Lean function to assertion-level arguments -/
374addedsyntax:max "#" term:max (assn_aexp:max)+ : assn_aexp
375added/-- Addition -/
376addedsyntax:65 assn_aexp:65 " + " assn_aexp:66 : assn_aexp
377added/-- Subtraction -/
378addedsyntax:65 assn_aexp:65 " - " assn_aexp:66 : assn_aexp
379added/-- Multiplication -/
380addedsyntax:70 assn_aexp:70 " * " assn_aexp:71 : assn_aexp
381added/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
382addedsyntax "(" assn_aexp ")" : assn_aexp
383added/-- Escape to Lean -/
384addedsyntax:max "~" term:max : assn_aexp
385added
386added/-- The grammar for Hoare logic assertions -/
387addeddeclare_syntax_cat assn
388added/-- Equality of arithmetic expressions -/
389addedsyntax:50 assn_aexp:51 " = " assn_aexp:51 : assn
390added/-- Disequality of arithmetic expressions -/
391addedsyntax:50 assn_aexp:51 " ≠ " assn_aexp:51 : assn
392added/-- Less than or equal -/
393addedsyntax:50 assn_aexp:51 " ≤ " assn_aexp:51 : assn
394added/-- Less than -/
395addedsyntax:50 assn_aexp:51 " < " assn_aexp:51 : assn
396added/-- Greater than or equal -/
397addedsyntax:50 assn_aexp:51 " ≥ " assn_aexp:51 : assn
398added/-- Greater than -/
399addedsyntax:50 assn_aexp:51 " > " assn_aexp:51 : assn
400added/-- Conjunction -/
401addedsyntax:35 assn:36 " ∧ " assn:35 : assn
402added/-- Disjunction -/
403addedsyntax:30 assn:31 " ∨ " assn:30 : assn
404added/-- Negation -/
405addedsyntax:40 "¬" assn:41 : assn
406added/-- Implication -/
407addedsyntax:25 assn:26 " → " assn:25 : assn
408added/-- Iff -/
409addedsyntax:20 assn:21 " ↔ " assn:21 : assn
410added/-- A bare identifier: an `Assertion`, a `Prop` (such as `True` and
411added`False`), or -- later in the chapter -- a `Bexp` -/
412addedsyntax:max ident : assn
413added/-- Parentheses for grouping -/
414addedsyntax "(" assn ")" : assn
415added/-- Escape to Lean -/
416addedsyntax:max "~" term:max : assn
417added
418added/-- Embed an assertion into a Lean term -/
419addedsyntax:max "{{" assn "}}" : term
420added/-- (Internal) embed an assertion-level arithmetic expression into a Lean
421addedterm -/
422addedsyntax:max "assnAexp " "{" assn_aexp "}" : term
423added
424added-- One small limitation of this approach is that we don't have an automatic
425added-- way to coerce a function application that appears within an assertion to
426added-- make appropriate use of the state when its arguments should be interpets as
427added-- Imp arithmetic expressions. Instead, we introduce a notation `#f e1 .. en`
428added-- that stands for `fun st => f (e1 st) .. (en st)`, letting us manually mark
429added-- such function calls when they're needed as part of an assertion.
430added
431added-- Note to developers:
432added-- NOTATION: This notation should come early so that later notations for
433added-- arithmetic expressions take precedence for printing. Otherwise
434added-- `{{ X + X }}` would print as `{{ #add X Y }}`.
435added
436addedopen Lean in
437addedmacro_rules
438added | `(assnAexp { $n:num }) => `(Aexp'.ofNat $n)
439added | `(assnAexp { $x:ident }) => `(($x : Aexp'))
440added | `(assnAexp { ~$e }) => `(($e : Aexp'))
441added | `(assnAexp { # $f $args* }) => do
442added let st := mkIdent `st
443added let mut r : Term := f
444added for a in args do
445added r ← `($r ((assnAexp { $a }) $st))
446added `(fun $st => $r)
447added | `(assnAexp { $a + $b }) => `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st + (assnAexp { $b }) st)
448added | `(assnAexp { $a - $b }) => `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st - (assnAexp { $b }) st)
449added | `(assnAexp { $a * $b }) => `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st * (assnAexp { $b }) st)
450added | `(assnAexp { ($a) }) => `(assnAexp { $a })
451added
452addedmacro_rules
453added | `({{ $a:assn_aexp = $b:assn_aexp }}) =>
454added `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st = (assnAexp { $b }) st)
455added | `({{ $a:assn_aexp ≠ $b:assn_aexp }}) =>
456added `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st ≠ (assnAexp { $b }) st)
457added | `({{ $a:assn_aexp ≤ $b:assn_aexp }}) =>
458added `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st ≤ (assnAexp { $b }) st)
459added | `({{ $a:assn_aexp < $b:assn_aexp }}) =>
460added `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st < (assnAexp { $b }) st)
461added | `({{ $a:assn_aexp ≥ $b:assn_aexp }}) =>
462added `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st ≥ (assnAexp { $b }) st)
463added | `({{ $a:assn_aexp > $b:assn_aexp }}) =>
464added `(fun st => (assnAexp { $a }) st > (assnAexp { $b }) st)
465added | `({{ $p ∧ $q }}) => `(fun st => ({{ $p }}) st ∧ ({{ $q }}) st)
466added | `({{ $p ∨ $q }}) => `(fun st => ({{ $p }}) st ∨ ({{ $q }}) st)
467added | `({{ ¬ $p }}) => `(fun st => ¬ ({{ $p }}) st)
468added | `({{ $p → $q }}) => `(fun st => ({{ $p }}) st → ({{ $q }}) st)
469added | `({{ $p ↔ $q }}) => `(fun st => ({{ $p }}) st ↔ ({{ $q }}) st)
470added | `({{ $x:ident }}) => `(($x : Assertion))
471added | `({{ ($p:assn) }}) => `({{ $p }})
472added | `({{ ~$e }}) => `(($e : Assertion))
473added
474added-- Occasionally we need to "escape" a raw Lean function to express a
475added-- particularly complicated assertion. We can do that using a `~` prefix, as
476added-- in `{{ ~(raw_lean) }}` -- the same escape convention that the `imp { … }`
477added-- notation uses.
478added
479added-- For example, `{{ ~(fun st => ∀ x, st[x] = 0) }}` indicates an assertion
480added-- that every variable maps to `0` in the given state.
481added
482added-- Note to developers:
483added-- NOTATION: SAZ 2024: It is important that this custom notation be at a
484added-- level higher than 1 when added to the `constr` grammar because it
485added-- interacts with the "application" case of `com` and the notation for
486added-- Hoare triples. That grammar parses embedded function arguments at level
487added-- 1. We never want `f {{P}}` to parse `{{P}}` as an assertion when used
488added-- in a command. Instead we want `{{ P }}` to "close" the Hoare triple.
489added--
490added-- `NOTATION: Note for Rocq custom grammar hackers. From what I can tell, the
491added-- Rocq LL(1) parser does left-factorize the grammar, *however* it uses a very
492added-- strict notion of what counts as "equal" for the purposes of the factorization.
493added-- In particular, a grammar entry might have a level,
494added-- as in [e custom assn at level 99] in the notation below. Leaving out the
495added-- "at level 99" is *semantically equivalent*, because the [assn] grammar starts
496added-- at that level, but omitting it will not work because the grammar for
497added-- Hoare triples below includes "at level 99" -- the [LEVEL "99"] part of the
498added-- grammar counts for factorization.
499added--
500added-- The upshot is that means that this notation and the Hoare triple notation
501added-- (which overlaps with [{{ _ }}]) must be changed in tandem and use identical
502added-- level specifications.`
503added
504added-- ### Example Assertions
505added
506added-- Here are some example assertions that take advantage of this new notation.
507added
508addednamespace ExamplePrettyAssertions
509addeddef assertion1 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 }}
510addeddef assertion2 : Assertion := {{ True }}
511addeddef assertion3 : Assertion := {{ False }}
512addeddef assertion4 : Assertion := {{ True ∨ False }}
513addeddef assertion5 : Assertion := {{ X ≤ Y }}
514addeddef assertion6 : Assertion := {{ X = 3 ∨ X ≤ Y }}
515addeddef assertion7 : Assertion := {{ Z = (#max X Y) }}
516addeddef assertion8 : Assertion := {{ Z * Z ≤ X
517added ∧ ¬ (((#Nat.succ Z) * (#Nat.succ Z)) ≤ X) }}
518addeddef assertion9 : Assertion := {{ #Nat.add X Y > #max Y X }}
519addedend ExamplePrettyAssertions
520added
521added-- ### Assertion Implication
522added
523added-- Given two assertions `P` and `Q`, we say that `P` *implies* `Q`, written
524added-- `P ->> Q`, if, whenever `P` holds in some state `st`, `Q` also holds.
525added
526addeddef AssertImplies (P Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
527added ∀ st, P st → Q st
528added
529added-- Note that the notation for *assertion implication* is analogous to the
530added-- "usual" Lean implication `→`.
531added
532addednotation:26 P:27 " ->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q
533added
534added-- We'll also want the "iff" variant of implication between assertions:
535added
536addednotation:26 P:27 " <<->> " Q:27 => AssertImplies P Q ∧ AssertImplies Q P
537added
538added-- Note to developers (Claude):
539added-- The Rocq source puts these notations in a `hoare_spec_scope`, with a
540added-- book comment explaining that "the `hoare_spec_scope` annotation tells
541added-- Rocq that this notation is not global but is intended to be used in
542added-- particular contexts." Lean has no notation scopes, so the notations are
543added-- simply global and that paragraph is omitted.
544added
545added-- ## Hoare Triples, Informally
546added
547added-- A *Hoare triple* is a claim about the state before and after executing a
548added-- command. The standard notation is
549added
550added-- {P} c {Q}
551added
552added-- meaning:
553added
554added-- - If command `c` begins execution in a state satisfying assertion `P`,
555added-- - and if `c` eventually terminates in some final state,
556added-- - then that final state will satisfy the assertion `Q`.
557added
558added-- Assertion `P` is called the *precondition* of the triple, and `Q` is the
559added-- *postcondition*.
560added
561added-- Because single braces are already used for other things in Lean, we'll
562added-- write Hoare triples with double braces:
563added
564added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
565added
566added-- For example,
567added
568added-- - The Hoare triple
569added
570added-- {{X = 0}} X := X + 1 {{X = 1}}
571added
572added-- states that command `X := X + 1` will transform a state in which `X = 0` to
573added-- a state in which `X = 1`.
574added
575added-- - On the other hand,
576added
577added-- ∀ m, {{X = m}} X := X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}
578added
579added-- is a *proposition* stating that the Hoare triple
580added-- `{{X = m}} X :=
581added-- X + 1 {{X = m + 1}}` is valid for any choice of `m`. Note
582added-- that `m` in the two assertions is a reference to the *Lean* variable `m`,
583added-- which is bound outside the Hoare triple.
584added
585added-- _Quiz:_
586added
587added-- Paraphrase the following in English.
588added
589added-- 1) {{True}} c {{X = 5}}
590added
591added-- 2) ∀ m, {{X = m}} c {{X = m + 5}}
592added
593added-- 3) {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
594added
595added-- 4) {{True}} c {{False}}
596added
597added-- 5) ∀ m,
598added-- {{X = m}}
599added-- c
600added-- {{Y = real_fact m}}
601added
602added-- 6) ∀ m,
603added-- {{X = m}}
604added-- c
605added-- {{(Z * Z) ≤ m ∧ ¬ ((Z + 1) * (Z + 1) ≤ m)}}
606added
607added-- _Quiz:_
608added
609added-- Is the following Hoare triple *valid* -- i.e., is the claimed relation
610added-- between `P`, `c`, and `Q` true?
611added
612added-- {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
613added
614added-- (A) Yes
615added
616added-- (B) No
617added
618added-- _Quiz:_
619added
620added-- What about this one?
621added
622added-- {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
623added
624added-- (A) Yes
625added
626added-- (B) No
627added
628added-- _Quiz:_
629added
630added-- What about this one?
631added
632added-- {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
633added
634added-- (A) Yes
635added
636added-- (B) No
637added
638added-- _Quiz:_
639added
640added-- What about this one?
641added
642added-- {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
643added
644added-- (A) Yes
645added
646added-- (B) No
647added
648added-- _Quiz:_
649added
650added-- What about this one?
651added
652added-- {{True}} skip {{False}}
653added
654added-- (A) Yes
655added
656added-- (B) No
657added
658added-- _Quiz:_
659added
660added-- What about this one?
661added
662added-- {{False}} skip {{True}}
663added
664added-- (A) Yes
665added
666added-- (B) No
667added
668added-- _Quiz:_
669added
670added-- What about this one?
671added
672added-- {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
673added
674added-- (A) Yes
675added
676added-- (B) No
677added
678added-- _Quiz:_
679added
680added-- This one?
681added
682added-- {{X = 0}}
683added-- while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
684added-- {{X = 1}}
685added
686added-- (A) Yes
687added
688added-- (B) No
689added
690added-- _Quiz:_
691added
692added-- This one?
693added
694added-- {{X = 1}}
695added-- while X ≠ 0 do X := X + 1 end
696added-- {{X = 100}}
697added
698added-- (A) Yes
699added
700added-- (B) No
701added
702added-- ### Exercise (1 star): valid_triples ⭐
703added
704added-- Which of the following Hoare triples are *valid* -- i.e., the claimed
705added-- relation between `P`, `c`, and `Q` is true?
706added
707added-- 1) {{True}} X := 5 {{X = 5}}
708added
709added-- 2) {{X = 2}} X := X + 1 {{X = 3}}
710added
711added-- 3) {{True}} X := 5; Y := 0 {{X = 5}}
712added
713added-- 4) {{X = 2 ∧ X = 3}} X := 5 {{X = 0}}
714added
715added-- 5) {{True}} skip {{False}}
716added
717added-- 6) {{False}} skip {{True}}
718added
719added-- 7) {{True}} while true do skip end {{False}}
720added
721added-- 8) {{X = 0}}
722added-- while X = 0 do X := X + 1 end
723added-- {{X = 1}}
724added
725added-- 9) {{X = 1}}
726added-- while X ≠ 0 do X := X + 1 end
727added-- {{X = 100}}
