731added-- ## Hoare Triples, Formally
732added
733added-- We formalize valid Hoare triples in Lean as follows:
734added
735addeddef ValidHoareTriple
736added (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
737added ∀ st st',
738added (st =[ c ]=> st') →
739added P st →
740added Q st'
741added
742added-- Note to developers:
743added-- `NOTATION: SAZ 2024 One trickiness of these notations is that we
744added-- want the [com] and [assn] grammars to be "open", so that they can
745added-- include expressions parsed by the full [constr] grammar of Rocq.
746added-- However, then there is a conflict of precedence of the
747added-- "application" cases:
748added--
749added-- The example " {{ True }} X := 0 {{ False }} " does not parse as
750added-- intended because the [com] grammar includes the capability of
751added-- parsing the (ill-typed) term "0 {{ False }}".
752added--
753added-- This means that the "application" for [com] should disallow
754added-- arguments at the level at which the [assn] grammar is included
755added-- in constr. The upshot is that this notation should be included
756added-- in the grammar at the *same* level as the assertion notation
757added-- [{{ P }}], which is 2.`
758added
759added-- Notation for Hoare triples. The command between the two assertions is
760added-- parsed with the same grammar as the `imp { … }` notation, so a command that
761added-- is a Lean variable (rather than concrete syntax) is spliced in with `~c`,
762added-- just as in the `st =[ c ]=> st'` notation.
763added
764added/-- Hoare triple: `{{ P }} c {{ Q }}` -/
765addedsyntax:40 "{{" assn "}}" atomic(ppHardSpace imp_com ppHardSpace "{{") assn "}}" : term
766added
767addedmacro_rules
768added | `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }}) =>
769added `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imp { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))
770added
771added-- Note to developers:
772added-- `HIDE: AAA: If I try to set the notation as {P} c {Q}, I get the
773added-- following error:
774added--
775added-- Error: A notation must include at least one symbol.
776added--
777added-- Maybe we could use other braces? For instance, I tried it with [P]
778added-- c [Q] and it seems to work (although I don't know how that would
779added-- affect the rest of the book).
780added--
781added-- BCP: Let's try with the "squashed" double braces for a while and
782added-- see if we like it.
783added--
784added-- P.S.
785added-- This works:
786added-- Notation "{ x }" := (x) (at level 0, x at level 99).
787added-- But this doesn't:
788added-- Notation "{ P } c { Q }" :=
789added-- (ValidHoareTriple P c Q)
790added-- (at level 0, P at level 99, c at level 99, Q at level 99)
791added-- : hoare_spec_scope.
792added-- Why??`
793added
794added-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_post_true ⭐
795added
796added-- Prove that if `Q` holds in every state, then any triple with `Q` as its
797added-- postcondition is valid.
798added
799addedtheorem hoare_post_true (P Q : Assertion) (c : Com) (h : ∀ st, Q st) :
800added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
801added all_goals
802added unfold ValidHoareTriple
803added intro st st' _heval _hp
804added apply h
805added
806added-- ### Exercise (1 star): hoare_pre_false ⭐
807added
808added-- Prove that if `P` holds in no state, then any triple with `P` as its
809added-- precondition is valid.
810added
811addedtheorem hoare_pre_false (P Q : Assertion) (c : Com) (h : ∀ st, ¬ (P st)) :
812added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
813added all_goals
814added unfold ValidHoareTriple
815added intro st st' _heval hp
816added apply h at hp
817added contradiction
818added
819added-- ## Proof Rules
820added
821added-- The goal of Hoare logic is to provide a *compositional* method for proving
822added-- the validity of specific Hoare triples. That is, we want the structure of a
823added-- program's correctness proof to mirror the structure of the program itself.
824added-- To this end, in the sections below, we'll introduce a rule for reasoning
825added-- about each of the different syntactic forms of commands in Imp -- one for
826added-- assignment, one for sequencing, one for conditionals, etc. -- plus a couple
827added-- of "structural" rules for gluing things together. We will then be able to
828added-- prove programs correct using these proof rules, without ever unfolding the
829added-- definition of `ValidHoareTriple`.
830added
831added-- ### Skip
832added
833added-- Since `skip` doesn't change the state, it preserves any assertion `P`:
834added
835added-- -------------------- (hoare_skip)
836added-- {{ P }} skip {{ P }}
837added
838addedtheorem hoare_skip (P : Assertion) :
839added {{P}} skip; {{P}} := by
840added intro st st' h hp
841added inversion h
842added assumption
843added
844added-- ### Sequencing
845added
846added-- If command `c1` takes any state where `P` holds to a state where `Q` holds,
847added-- and if `c2` takes any state where `Q` holds to one where `R` holds, then
848added-- doing `c1` followed by `c2` will take any state where `P` holds to one
849added-- where `R` holds:
850added
851added-- {{ P }} c1 {{ Q }}
852added-- {{ Q }} c2 {{ R }}
853added-- ---------------------- (hoare_seq)
854added-- {{ P }} c1;c2 {{ R }}
855added
856addedtheorem hoare_seq (P Q R : Assertion) (c1 c2 : Com)
857added (h1 : {{Q}} ~c2 {{R}}) (h2 : {{P}} ~c1 {{Q}}) :
858added {{P}} ~c1 ~c2 {{R}} := by
859added intro st st' h12 pre
860added inversion h12 with
861added | seq st'' hc1 hc2 =>
862added exact h1 _ _ hc2 (h2 _ _ hc1 pre)
863added
864added-- Note that, in the formal rule `hoare_seq`, the premises are given in
865added-- backwards order (`c2` before `c1`). This matches the natural flow of
866added-- information in many of the situations where we'll use the rule, since the
867added-- natural way to construct a Hoare-logic proof is to begin at the end of the
868added-- program (with the final postcondition) and push postconditions backwards
869added-- through commands until we reach the beginning.
870added
871added-- ### Assignment
872added
873added-- The rule for assignment is the most fundamental of the Hoare logic proof
874added-- rules. Here's how it works.
875added
876added-- Consider this incomplete Hoare triple:
877added
878added-- {{ ??? }} X := Y {{ X = 1 }}
879added
880added-- We want to assign `Y` to `X` and finish in a state where `X` is `1`. What
881added-- could the precondition be?
882added
883added-- One possibility is `Y = 1`, because if `Y` is already `1` then assigning it
884added-- to `X` causes `X` to be `1`. That leads to a valid Hoare triple:
885added
886added-- {{ Y = 1 }} X := Y {{ X = 1 }}
887added
888added-- It may seem as though coming up with that precondition must have taken some
889added-- clever thought. But there is a mechanical way we could have done it: if we
890added-- take the postcondition `X = 1` and in it replace `X` with `Y`---that is,
891added-- replace the left-hand side of the assignment statement with the right-hand
892added-- side---we get the precondition, `Y = 1`.
893added
894added-- That same idea works in more complicated cases. For example:
895added
896added-- {{ ??? }} X := X + Y {{ X = 1 }}
897added
898added-- If we replace the `X` in `X = 1` with `X + Y`, we get `X + Y = 1`. That
899added-- again leads to a valid Hoare triple:
900added
901added-- {{ X + Y = 1 }} X := X + Y {{ X = 1 }}
902added
903added-- Why does this technique work? The postcondition identifies some property
904added-- `P` that we want to hold of the variable `X` being assigned. In this case,
905added-- `P` is "equals `1`". To complete the triple and make it valid, we need to
906added-- identify a precondition that guarantees that property will hold of `X`.
907added-- Such a precondition must ensure that the same property holds of *whatever
908added-- is being assigned to* `X`. So, in the example, we need "equals `1`" to hold
909added-- of `X + Y`. That's exactly what the technique guarantees.
910added
911added-- In general, the postcondition could be some arbitrary assertion `Q`, and
912added-- the right-hand side of the assignment could be some arbitrary arithmetic
913added-- expression `a`:
914added
915added-- {{ ??? }} X := a {{ Q }}
916added
917added-- The precondition would then be `Q`, but with any occurrences of `X` in it
918added-- replaced by `a`.
919added
920added-- Let's introduce a notation for this idea of replacing occurrences: Define
921added-- `Q \[X ↦ a`] to mean "`Q` where `a` is substituted in place of `X`".
922added
923added-- This yields the Hoare logic rule for assignment:
924added
925added-- {{ Q [X ↦ a] }} X := a {{ Q }}
926added
927added-- One way of reading this rule is: If you want statement `X := a` to
928added-- terminate in a state that satisfies assertion `Q`, then it suffices to
929added-- start in a state that also satisfies `Q`, except where `a` is substituted
930added-- for every occurrence of `X`.
931added
932added-- To many people, this rule seems "backwards" at first, because it proceeds
933added-- from the postcondition to the precondition. Actually it makes good sense to
934added-- go in this direction: the postcondition is often what is more important,
935added-- because it characterizes what will be true after running the code.
936added
937added-- Nonetheless, it's also possible to formulate a "forward" assignment rule.
938added-- We'll do that later in some exercises.
939added
940added-- Here are some valid instances of the assignment rule:
941added
942added-- {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }} (that is, X + 1 ≤ 5)
943added-- X := X + 1
944added-- {{ X ≤ 5 }}
945added
946added-- {{ (X = 3) [X ↦ 3] }} (that is, 3 = 3)
947added-- X := 3
948added-- {{ X = 3 }}
949added
950added-- {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}. (that is, 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5)
951added-- X := 3
952added-- {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }}
953added
954added-- To formalize the rule, we must first formalize the idea of "substituting an
955added-- expression for an Imp variable in an assertion", which we refer to as
956added-- assertion substitution, or `Assertion.sub`.
957added
958added-- Intuitively, given a proposition `P`, a variable `X`, and an arithmetic
959added-- expression `a`, we want to derive another proposition `P'` that is just the
960added-- same as `P` except that `P'` should mention `a` wherever `P` mentions `X`.
961added
962added-- This operation is related to the idea of substituting Imp expressions for
963added-- Imp variables that we saw in *Equiv* (`subst_aexp` and friends). The
964added-- difference is that, here, `P` is an arbitrary Lean assertion, so we can't
965added-- directly "edit" its text.
966added
967added-- However, we can achieve the same effect by evaluating `P` in an updated
968added-- state, defined as follows:
969added
970addeddef Assertion.sub (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) : Assertion :=
971added fun (st : State) => P (x →ₜ a.eval st ; st)
972added
973added-- Note to developers (before next release):
974added-- This concrete syntax is hard to read in comments because of all the
975added-- square brackets. Something like `P with X ↦ a` would be much better. I
976added-- guess the same will apply to the lambda-calculus chapters... BCP 25: I
977added-- still think this is a good idea, and I had a quick go at implementing
978added-- it, but did not succeed yet.
979added
980added/-- Assertion substitution: `P [X ↦ a]` -/
981addedsyntax:100 assn:100 " [" ident " ↦ " imp_aexp "]" : assn
982added
983addedmacro_rules
984added | `({{ $P [$x ↦ $a] }}) => `(Assertion.sub $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $P }}))
985added
986added-- This notation allows us to write this operation as:
987added
988added-- P [ X ↦ a ]
989added
990added-- That is, `P [X ↦ a]` stands for an assertion -- let's call it `P'` -- that
991added-- behaves just like `P` except that, wherever `P` looks up the variable `X`
992added-- in the current state, `P'` instead uses the value of the expression `a`.
993added
994added-- To see how this works in more detail, let's calculate what happens with a
995added-- couple of examples. First, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3]` -- that is,
996added-- more formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
997added
998added-- fun st =>
999added-- (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1000added-- (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st 3 ; st),
1001added
1002added-- which simplifies to
1003added
1004added-- fun st =>
1005added-- (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1006added-- (X →ₜ 3 ; st)
1007added
1008added-- and further simplifies to
1009added
1010added-- fun st =>
1011added-- ((X →ₜ 3 ; st)[X]) ≤ 5
1012added
1013added-- and finally to
1014added
1015added-- fun st =>
1016added-- 3 ≤ 5.
1017added
1018added-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `3` is less than or equal to `5` (as
1019added-- expected).
1020added
1021added-- For a more interesting example, suppose `P'` is `(X ≤ 5) [X ↦
1022added-- X + 1]`.
1023added-- Formally, `P'` is the Lean expression
1024added
1025added-- fun st =>
1026added-- (fun st' => st'[X] ≤ 5)
1027added-- (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st),
1028added
1029added-- which simplifies to
1030added
1031added-- fun st =>
1032added-- (X →ₜ Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 }) ; st)[X] ≤ 5
1033added
1034added-- and further simplifies to
1035added
1036added-- fun st =>
1037added-- (Aexp.eval st (aexp { X + 1 })) ≤ 5.
1038added
1039added-- That is, `P'` is the assertion that `X + 1` is at most `5`.
1040added
1041added-- We can demonstrate formally that we have captured intuitive meaning of
1042added-- "assertion subsitution" by proving some example logical equivalences:
1043added
1044addednamespace ExampleAssertionSub
1045addedexample :
1046added {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }} <<->> {{ 3 ≤ 5 }} := by
1047added constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
1048added
1049addedexample :
1050added {{ (X ≤ 5) [X ↦ X + 1] }} <<->> {{ (X + 1) ≤ 5 }} := by
1051added constructor <;> (unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub; intro st h; exact h)
1052added
1053addedend ExampleAssertionSub
1054added
1055added-- ### Printing Assertions
1056added
1057added-- As in the Imp chapter, the assertion notations above are *input* only: Lean
1058added-- reads `{{ X ≤ 5 }}` but still prints the underlying function. The
1059added-- delaborators below close the loop for the common cases: Hoare triples,
1060added-- `->>` implications, and assertion substitutions are printed back in their
1061added-- concrete notation, and an assertion Lean cannot rebuild falls back to the
1062added-- `~` escape (or, ultimately, to the raw term). As before, there is no need
1063added-- to understand the details, and everything can be switched off with
1064added-- `set_option pp.notation false`.
1065added
1066added-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: printing assertions back
1067added
1068addednamespace Assn.Delab
1069addedopen Lean PrettyPrinter Delaborator SubExpr Parenthesizer Imp.Delab
1070added
1071added/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `assn_aexp` output according to the grammar's
1072addedprecedences. -/
1073added@[category_parenthesizer assn_aexp]
1074addeddef assn_aexp.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
1075added maybeParenthesize `assn_aexp true wrapParens prec <|
1076added parenthesizeCategoryCore `assn_aexp prec
1077addedwhere
1078added wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
1079added let pstx ← `(assn_aexp| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
1080added return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
1081added
1082added/-- Re-inserts parentheses in `assn` output according to the grammar's
1083addedprecedences. -/
1084added@[category_parenthesizer assn]
1085addeddef assn.parenthesizer : CategoryParenthesizer | prec => do
1086added maybeParenthesize `assn true wrapParens prec <|
1087added parenthesizeCategoryCore `assn prec
1088addedwhere
1089added wrapParens (stx : Syntax) : Syntax := Unhygienic.run do
1090added let pstx ← `(assn| ($(⟨stx⟩)))
1091added return pstx.raw.setInfo (SourceInfo.fromRef stx)
1092added
1093added/-- Print the focused term as a bare identifier if it delaborates to one,
1094addedand with the `~` escape otherwise. -/
1095addeddef identOrEscapeAexp : DelabM (TSyntax `assn_aexp) := do
1096added match ← delab with
1097added | `($x:ident) => `(assn_aexp| $x:ident)
1098added | t => `(assn_aexp| ~$t)
1099added
1100added/-- Print the focused term as a bare identifier if it delaborates to one,
1101addedand with the `~` escape otherwise. -/
1102addeddef identOrEscapeAssn : DelabM (TSyntax `assn) := do
1103added match ← delab with
1104added | `($x:ident) => `(assn| $x:ident)
1105added | t => `(assn| ~$t)
1106added
1107added/-- Rebuild `assn_aexp` syntax from an `Aexp` (the argument of the
1108added`Aexp'.ofAexp` coercion). -/
1109addedpartial def delabAexpAsAssn : DelabM (TSyntax `assn_aexp) := do
1110added let stx ←
1111added match_expr ← getExpr with
1112added | Aexp.num _ =>
1113added match (← withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
1114added | some v => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString v) |>.raw⟩
1115added | none => identOrEscapeAexp
1116added | Aexp.id _ =>
1117added match ← withAppArg getExpr with
1118added | .const nm _ => `(assn_aexp| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
1119added | _ => identOrEscapeAexp
1120added | Aexp.plus _ _ =>
1121added let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpAsAssn
1122added let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpAsAssn
1123added `(assn_aexp| $s1 + $s2)
1124added | Aexp.minus _ _ =>
1125added let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpAsAssn
1126added let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpAsAssn
1127added `(assn_aexp| $s1 - $s2)
1128added | Aexp.mult _ _ =>
1129added let s1 ← withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpAsAssn
1130added let s2 ← withAppArg delabAexpAsAssn
1131added `(assn_aexp| $s1 * $s2)
1132added | _ => identOrEscapeAexp
1133added annAsTerm stx
1134added
1135addedmutual
1136added
1137added/-- Rebuild `assn_aexp` syntax from an assertion-level numeric value -- the
1138addedbody form the `{{ … }}` macros produce, applied to the state variable. -/
1139addedpartial def delabAssnAexpVal : DelabM (TSyntax `assn_aexp) := do
1140added let e ← getExpr
1141added let stx ←
1142added match_expr e with
1143added | HAdd.hAdd _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
1144added let s1 ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssnAexpVal
1145added let s2 ← withNaryArg 5 delabAssnAexpVal
1146added `(assn_aexp| $s1 + $s2)
1147added | HSub.hSub _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
1148added let s1 ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssnAexpVal
1149added let s2 ← withNaryArg 5 delabAssnAexpVal
1150added `(assn_aexp| $s1 - $s2)
1151added | HMul.hMul _ _ _ _ _ _ =>
1152added let s1 ← withNaryArg 4 delabAssnAexpVal
1153added let s2 ← withNaryArg 5 delabAssnAexpVal
1154added `(assn_aexp| $s1 * $s2)
1155added | _ =>
1156added let .app f v := e | failure
1157added guard v.isFVar
1158added match_expr f with
1159added | Aexp'.ofNat _ =>
1160added match (← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr).nat? with
1161added | some val => pure ⟨Syntax.mkNumLit (toString val) |>.raw⟩
1162added | none => withAppFn <| withAppArg identOrEscapeAexp
1163added | Aexp'.ofAexp _ => withAppFn <| withAppArg delabAexpAsAssn
1164added | _ =>
1165added if f.isLambda then
1166added withAppFn do withBindingBody (← getExpr).bindingName! delabAssnAexpVal
1167added else
1168added withAppFn identOrEscapeAexp
1169added annAsTerm stx
1170added
1171added/-- Rebuild `assn` syntax from an assertion body -- the proposition the
1172added`{{ … }}` macros produce, applied to the state variable. -/
1173addedpartial def delabAssnVal : DelabM (TSyntax `assn) := do
1174added let e ← getExpr
1175added let stx ←
1176added match_expr e with
1177added | Eq _ _ _ =>
1178added let s1 ← withNaryArg 1 delabAssnAexpVal
1179added let s2 ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnAexpVal
1180added `(assn| $s1:assn_aexp = $s2:assn_aexp)
1181added | Ne _ _ _ =>
1182added let s1 ← withNaryArg 1 delabAssnAexpVal
1183added let s2 ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnAexpVal
1184added `(assn| $s1:assn_aexp ≠ $s2:assn_aexp)
1185added | LE.le _ _ _ _ =>
1186added let s1 ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnAexpVal
1187added let s2 ← withNaryArg 3 delabAssnAexpVal
1188added `(assn| $s1:assn_aexp ≤ $s2:assn_aexp)
1189added | LT.lt _ _ _ _ =>
1190added let s1 ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnAexpVal
1191added let s2 ← withNaryArg 3 delabAssnAexpVal
1192added `(assn| $s1:assn_aexp < $s2:assn_aexp)
1193added | GE.ge _ _ _ _ =>
1194added let s1 ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnAexpVal
1195added let s2 ← withNaryArg 3 delabAssnAexpVal
1196added `(assn| $s1:assn_aexp ≥ $s2:assn_aexp)
1197added | GT.gt _ _ _ _ =>
1198added let s1 ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnAexpVal
1199added let s2 ← withNaryArg 3 delabAssnAexpVal
1200added `(assn| $s1:assn_aexp > $s2:assn_aexp)
1201added | And _ _ =>
1202added let s1 ← withNaryArg 0 delabAssnVal
1203added let s2 ← withNaryArg 1 delabAssnVal
1204added `(assn| $s1 ∧ $s2)
1205added | Or _ _ =>
1206added let s1 ← withNaryArg 0 delabAssnVal
1207added let s2 ← withNaryArg 1 delabAssnVal
1208added `(assn| $s1 ∨ $s2)
1209added | Iff _ _ =>
1210added let s1 ← withNaryArg 0 delabAssnVal
1211added let s2 ← withNaryArg 1 delabAssnVal
1212added `(assn| $s1 ↔ $s2)
1213added | Not _ =>
1214added `(assn| ¬$(← withAppArg delabAssnVal))
1215added | _ =>
1216added if e.isArrow then
1217added let s1 ← withBindingDomain delabAssnVal
1218added let s2 ← withBindingBody e.bindingName! delabAssnVal
1219added `(assn| $s1 → $s2)
1220added else
1221added let .app f v := e | failure
1222added guard v.isFVar
1223added match_expr f with
1224added | Assertion.ofProp _ =>
1225added match ← withAppFn <| withAppArg getExpr with
1226added | .const nm _ => `(assn| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
1227added | _ => withAppFn <| withAppArg identOrEscapeAssn
1228added | Assertion.sub _ _ _ => withAppFn delabSubInner
1229added | _ =>
1230added if f.isLambda then
1231added withAppFn do withBindingBody (← getExpr).bindingName! delabAssnVal
1232added else
1233added withAppFn identOrEscapeAssn
1234added annAsTerm stx
1235added
1236added/-- Rebuild the substitution notation from an `Assertion.sub` application. -/
1237addedpartial def delabSubInner : DelabM (TSyntax `assn) := do
1238added let .const nm _ ← withNaryArg 0 getExpr | failure
1239added let a ← withNaryArg 1 delabAexpInner
1240added let P ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnFun
1241added `(assn| $P [$(mkIdent nm):ident ↦ $a:imp_aexp])
1242added
1243added/-- Rebuild `assn` syntax from an `Assertion`-valued term. -/
1244addedpartial def delabAssnFun : DelabM (TSyntax `assn) := do
1245added let e ← getExpr
1246added let stx ←
1247added match_expr e with
1248added | Assertion.ofProp _ =>
1249added match ← withAppArg getExpr with
1250added | .const nm _ => `(assn| $(mkIdent nm):ident)
1251added | _ => withAppArg identOrEscapeAssn
1252added | Assertion.sub _ _ _ => delabSubInner
1253added | _ =>
1254added if e.isLambda then
1255added withBindingBody e.bindingName! delabAssnVal
1256added else
1257added identOrEscapeAssn
1258added annAsTerm stx
1259added
1260addedend
1261added
1262added/-- Rebuild `assn` syntax from an `Assertion`, falling back to the escaped
1263addedraw term. -/
1264addeddef delabAssnTotal : DelabM (TSyntax `assn) :=
1265added delabAssnFun <|> identOrEscapeAssn
1266added
1267added-- _Details:_ Notation encoding: registering the delaborators
1268added
1269added@[delab app.ValidHoareTriple]
1270addeddef delabTriple : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1271added guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``ValidHoareTriple 3
1272added let P ← withNaryArg 0 delabAssnTotal
1273added let c ← withNaryArg 1 delabComInner
1274added let Q ← withNaryArg 2 delabAssnTotal
1275added `({{ $P }} $c:imp_com {{ $Q }})
1276added
1277added@[delab app.AssertImplies]
1278addeddef delabAssertImplies : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1279added guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``AssertImplies 2
1280added let P ← withNaryArg 0 delabAssnTotal
1281added let Q ← withNaryArg 1 delabAssnTotal
1282added `({{ $P }} ->> {{ $Q }})
1283added
1284added@[delab app.Assertion.sub]
1285addeddef delabSub : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1286added guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``Assertion.sub 3
1287added `({{ $(← delabSubInner) }})
1288added
1289added@[delab app.Assertion.ofProp]
1290addeddef delabOfProp : Delab := whenPPOption getPPNotation do
1291added guard <| (← getExpr).isAppOfArity ``Assertion.ofProp 1
1292added `({{ $(← delabAssnFun) }})
1293added
1294addedend Assn.Delab
1295added
1296added-- Now, using the substitution operation we've just defined, we can give the
1297added-- precise proof rule for assignment:
1298added
1299added-- ---------------------------- (hoare_asgn)
1300added-- {{Q [X ↦ a]}} X := a {{Q}}
1301added
1302added-- We can prove formally that this rule is indeed valid.
1303added
1304addedtheorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
1305added {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a; {{Q}} := by
1306added intro st st' hE hQ
1307added inversion hE with
1308added | asgn n h =>
1309added subst h
1310added exact hQ
1311added
1312added-- Here's a first formal proof of a Hoare triple using this rule.
1313added
1314addedtheorem assertion_sub_example :
1315added {{(X < 5) [X ↦ X + 1]}}
1316added X := X + 1;
1317added {{X < 5}} := by
1318added apply hoare_asgn
1319added
1320added-- Of course, we'd probably prefer to work with this simpler triple:
1321added
1322added-- {{X < 4}} X := X + 1 {{X < 5}}
1323added
1324added-- We will see how to do so in the next section.
1325added
1326added-- Several proofs below use the facts about total-map updates proved in the
1327added-- *Typeclasses* chapter -- `TotalMap.update_eq`, `TotalMap.update_neq`,
1328added-- `TotalMap.update_shadow`, `TotalMap.update_same`, and
1329added-- `TotalMap.update_permute`. Make sure you understand their statements.
1330added
1331added-- Complete these Hoare triples by providing an appropriate precondition using
1332added-- `exists`, then prove then with `apply
1333added-- hoare_asgn`. If you find that tactic
1334added-- doesn't suffice, double check that you have completed the triple properly.
1335added
1336added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_examples1 ⭐⭐
1337added
1338addedtheorem hoare_asgn_examples1 :
1339added ∃ P : Assertion,
1340added {{ ~P }}
1341added X := 2 * X;
1342added {{ X ≤ 10 }} := by
1343added all_goals
1344added exists {{ (X ≤ 10) [X ↦ 2 * X] }}
1345added apply hoare_asgn
1346added
1347added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_examples2 ⭐⭐
1348added
1349addedtheorem hoare_asgn_examples2 :
1350added ∃ P : Assertion,
1351added {{ ~P }}
1352added X := 3;
1353added {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }} := by
1354added all_goals
1355added exists {{ (0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5) [X ↦ 3] }}
1356added apply hoare_asgn
1357added
1358added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_wrong ⭐⭐
1359added
1360added-- The assignment rule looks backward to almost everyone the first time they
1361added-- see it. If it still seems puzzling to you, it may help to think a little
1362added-- about alternative "forward" rules. Here is a seemingly natural one:
1363added
1364added-- ------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_wrong)
1365added-- {{ True }} X := a {{ X = a }}
1366added
1367added-- Give a counterexample showing that this rule is incorrect and use it to
1368added-- complete the proof below, showing that it is really a counterexample.
1369added-- (Hint: The rule universally quantifies over the arithmetic expression `a`,
1370added-- so your counterexample needs to exhibit an `a` for which the rule doesn't
1371added-- work.)
1372added
1373addedtheorem hoare_asgn_wrong : ∃ a : Aexp,
1374added ¬ {{ True }} X := ~a; {{ X = ~a }} := by
1375added all_goals
1376added exists aexp { X + 1 }
1377added intro hc
1378added unfold ValidHoareTriple at hc
1379added have h2 : (X →ₜ 1 ; ∅)[X] = (aexp { X + 1 }).eval (X →ₜ 1 ; ∅) := by
1380added apply hc ∅ (X →ₜ 1 ; ∅)
1381added · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1382added · exact True.intro
1383added simp [TotalMap.update_eq] at h2
1384added
1385added-- If `a` itself mentions `X`, then the value of `a` may be different in the
1386added-- final state because of this update. For example, if `a` is `X + 1`, then
1387added-- setting `X` to `a` certainly does not achieve the postcondition
1388added-- `X = X + 1`! The underlying problem is that the state in which the
1389added-- postcondition will be checked is different than the state in which `a` was
1390added-- evaluated when it was assigned to `X`.
1391added
1392added-- ### Exercise (3 stars): hoare_asgn_fwd (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐
1393added
1394added-- By using a *parameter* `m` (a Lean number) to remember the original value
1395added-- of `X` we can define a Hoare rule for assignment that does, intuitively,
1396added-- "work forwards" rather than backwards.
1397added
1398added-- ------------------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_fwd)
1399added-- {{fun st => P st ∧ st[X] = m}}
1400added-- X := a
1401added-- {{fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧ st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}
1402added
1403added-- Note that we need to write out the postcondition in "desugared" form,
1404added-- because it needs to talk about two different states: we use the original
1405added-- value of `X` to reconstruct the state `st'` before the assignment took
1406added-- place. (Also note that this rule is more complicated than `hoare_asgn`!)
1407added
1408added-- Prove that this rule is correct.
1409added
1410added-- Note to developers:
1411added-- HIDE: BCP 21: Could we make the precondition use compact notation, at
1412added-- least?
1413added--
1414added-- HIDE: SAZ 2024 - this version of the syntax does let us use the compact
1415added-- notation for the precondition, but it comes at the cost of having to
1416added-- "escape" the function in the postcondition.
1417added
1418addedtheorem hoare_asgn_fwd (m : Nat) (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) :
1419added {{~P ∧ X = m}}
1420added X := ~a;
1421added {{ ~(fun st => P (X →ₜ m ; st)
1422added ∧ st[X] = a.eval (X →ₜ m ; st)) }} := by
1423added all_goals
1424added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1425added intro st st' heval hpre
1426added inversion heval with
1427added | asgn n h =>
1428added obtain ⟨hp, hx⟩ := hpre
1429added subst h
1430added have hx' : st[X] = m := hx
1431added rw [← hx', TotalMap.update_eq, TotalMap.update_shadow,
1432added TotalMap.update_same]
1433added exact ⟨hp, rfl⟩
1434added
1435added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_fwd_exists (Advanced) ⭐⭐
1436added
1437added-- Another way to define a forward rule for assignment is to existentially
1438added-- quantify over the previous value of the assigned variable. Prove that it is
1439added-- correct.
1440added
1441added-- ------------------------------------ (hoare_asgn_fwd_exists)
1442added-- {{fun st => P st}}
1443added-- X := a
1444added-- {{fun st => ∃ m, P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧
1445added-- st[X] = Aexp.eval (X →ₜ m ; st) a }}
1446added
1447addedtheorem hoare_asgn_fwd_exists (a : Aexp) (P : Assertion) :
1448added {{ ~P }}
1449added X := ~a;
1450added {{ ~(fun st => ∃ m, P (X →ₜ m ; st) ∧
1451added st[X] = a.eval (X →ₜ m ; st)) }} := by
1452added all_goals
1453added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1454added intro st st' heval hpre
1455added inversion heval with
1456added | asgn n h =>
1457added subst h
1458added exists st[X]
1459added rw [TotalMap.update_eq, TotalMap.update_shadow, TotalMap.update_same]
1460added exact ⟨hpre, rfl⟩
1461added
1462added-- ### Consequence
1463added
1464added-- Sometimes the preconditions and postconditions we get from the Hoare rules
1465added-- won't quite be the ones we want in the particular situation at hand -- they
1466added-- may be logically equivalent but have a different syntactic form that fails
1467added-- to unify with the goal we are trying to prove, or they actually may be
1468added-- logically weaker (for preconditions) or stronger (for postconditions) than
1469added-- what we need.
1470added
1471added-- For instance,
1472added
1473added-- {{(X = 3) [X ↦ 3]}} X := 3 {{X = 3}},
1474added
1475added-- follows directly from the assignment rule, but
1476added
1477added-- {{True}} X := 3 {{X = 3}}
1478added
1479added-- does not. This triple is valid, but it is not an instance of `hoare_asgn`
1480added-- because `True` and `(X = 3) \[X ↦ 3`] are not syntactically equal
1481added-- assertions.
1482added
1483added-- However, they are logically *equivalent*, so if one triple is valid, then
1484added-- the other must certainly be as well. We can capture this observation with
1485added-- the following rule:
1486added
1487added-- {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1488added-- P <<->> P'
1489added-- ---------------------
1490added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1491added
1492added-- Taking this line of thought a bit further, we can see that strengthening
1493added-- the precondition or weakening the postcondition of a valid triple always
1494added-- produces another valid triple. This observation is captured by two *Rules
1495added-- of Consequence*.
1496added
1497added-- {{P'}} c {{Q}}
1498added-- P ->> P'
1499added-- ----------------------------- (hoare_consequence_pre)
1500added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1501added
1502added-- {{P}} c {{Q'}}
1503added-- Q' ->> Q
1504added-- ----------------------------- (hoare_consequence_post)
1505added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1506added
1507added-- Here are the formal versions:
1508added
1509addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1510added (hhoare : {{P'}} ~c {{Q}}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1511added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
1512added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1513added intro st st' heval hpre
1514added apply hhoare st st'
1515added · assumption
1516added · apply himp
1517added assumption
1518added
1519addedtheorem hoare_consequence_post (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1520added (hhoare : {{P}} ~c {{Q'}}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1521added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
1522added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1523added intro st st' heval hpre
1524added apply himp
1525added apply hhoare st st'
1526added · assumption
1527added · assumption
1528added
1529added-- For example, we can use the first consequence rule like this:
1530added
1531added-- {{ True }} ->>
1532added-- {{ (X = 1) [X ↦ 1] }}
1533added-- X := 1
1534added-- {{ X = 1 }}
1535added
1536added-- Or, formally...
1537added
1538addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1 :
1539added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1540added all_goals
1541added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1542added · apply hoare_asgn
1543added · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1544added intro st _
1545added rfl
1546added
1547added-- We can also use it to prove the example mentioned earlier.
1548added
1549added-- {{ X < 4 }} ->>
1550added-- {{ (X < 5)[X ↦ X + 1] }}
1551added-- X := X + 1
1552added-- {{ X < 5 }}
1553added
1554added-- Or, formally ...
1555added
1556addedtheorem assertion_sub_example2 :
1557added {{X < 4}}
1558added X := X + 1;
1559added {{X < 5}} := by
1560added all_goals
1561added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1562added · apply hoare_asgn
1563added · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1564added intro st h
1565added simp [Aexp'.ofAexp, Aexp'.ofNat, TotalMap.update_eq] at *
1566added lia
1567added
1568added-- Finally, here is a combined rule of consequence that allows us to vary both
1569added-- the precondition and the postcondition.
1570added
1571added-- {{P'}} c {{Q'}}
1572added-- P ->> P'
1573added-- Q' ->> Q
1574added-- ----------------------------- (hoare_consequence)
1575added-- {{P}} c {{Q}}
1576added
1577addedtheorem hoare_consequence (P P' Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1578added (htriple : {{P'}} ~c {{Q'}}) (hpre : P ->> P') (hpost : Q' ->> Q) :
1579added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
1580added apply hoare_consequence_pre (P' := P')
1581added · apply hoare_consequence_post (Q' := Q')
1582added · assumption
1583added · assumption
1584added · assumption
1585added
1586added-- ### Automation
1587added
1588added-- Many of the proofs we have done so far with Hoare triples can be
1589added-- streamlined using the automation techniques that we introduced in the
1590added-- *Automation* chapter of *Logical Foundations*.
1591added
1592added-- Recall that the `simp` tactic can be told to unfold definitions as part of
1593added-- its simplifications. The definitions we keep needing to unfold in this
1594added-- chapter are `ValidHoareTriple`, `AssertImplies`, `Assertion.sub`, the
1595added-- lifting functions `Assertion.ofProp`, `Aexp'.ofNat`, and `Aexp'.ofAexp`,
1596added-- and the total-map operations. We'll pass these to `simp` explicitly below
1597added-- (and shortly package the recipe up as a tactic of our own).
1598added
1599added-- Note to developers (Claude):
1600added-- The Rocq source here registers
1601added-- `Hint Unfold assert_implies assertion_sub
1602added-- t_update : core` for `auto`.
1603added-- That only widens `auto`'s search (unlike the `Arguments /.` commands,
1604added-- it does not affect `simpl`), so its Lean counterpart is the
1605added-- `assertion_auto` tactic's simp list below -- not global `@[simp]`
1606added-- lemmas as for the notation wrappers, whose folded names carry no
1607added-- meaning in goals the way `->>` and `Assertion.sub` do.
1608added
1609added-- The proof of `hoare_consequence_pre`, repeated below, looks like an
1610added-- opportune place for automation, because all it does is `unfold`, `intro`,
1611added-- and `apply`. (It uses `assumption`, too, but that's just application of a
1612added-- hypothesis.)
1613added
1614addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1615added (hhoare : {{P'}} ~c {{Q}}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1616added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
1617added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1618added intro st st' heval hpre
1619added apply hhoare st st'
1620added · assumption
1621added · apply himp
1622added assumption
1623added
1624added-- Notice that this proof passes the states `st` and `st'` to `apply
1625added-- hhoare`
1626added-- explicitly. We didn't actually need to: when an argument of the applied
1627added-- theorem is not determined by the goal, `apply` introduces a *metavariable*
1628added-- `?st` as a placeholder and lets a later step of the proof determine it.
1629added-- Here, `assumption` instantiates `?st` with `st` when it discovers `st` in
1630added-- the assumption `heval`. Using `apply` this way is like telling Lean, "Be
1631added-- patient: The missing part is going to be filled in later in the proof."
1632added
1633addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1634added (hhoare : {{P'}} ~c {{Q}}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1635added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
1636added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1637added intro st st' heval hpre
1638added apply hhoare
1639added · assumption
1640added · apply himp
1641added assumption
1642added
1643added-- Since the remaining steps just apply hypotheses to each other, the entire
1644added-- proof can actually be compressed into a single line, by writing the term
1645added-- that `exact`ly proves the conclusion.
1646added
1647addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre'''' (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
1648added (hhoare : {{P'}} ~c {{Q}}) (himp : P ->> P') :
1649added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
1650added intro st st' heval hpre
1651added exact hhoare st st' heval (himp st hpre)
1652added
1653added-- Of course, it's hard to write such a one-liner without having gone through
1654added-- the original proof of `hoare_consequence_pre` to see the steps it used. But
1655added-- now that we know the shape of the argument, it's a good bet that the same
1656added-- trick will also work for `hoare_consequence_post`.
1657added
1658addedtheorem hoare_consequence_post' (P Q Q' : Assertion) (c : Com)
1659added (hhoare : {{P}} ~c {{Q'}}) (himp : Q' ->> Q) :
1660added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
1661added intro st st' heval hpre
1662added exact himp st' (hhoare st st' heval hpre)
1663added
1664added-- We can also use a metavariable to streamline a proof
1665added-- (`hoare_asgn_example1`), that we did earlier as an example of using the
1666added-- consequence rule:
1667added
1668addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1' :
1669added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1670added apply hoare_consequence_pre -- no need to state an assertion
1671added · apply hoare_asgn
1672added · unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub
1673added intro st _
1674added rfl
1675added
1676added-- The final bullet of that proof also looks like a candidate for automation.
1677added
1678addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1'' :
1679added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1680added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1681added · apply hoare_asgn
1682added · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, Assertion.ofProp, Aexp'.ofNat,
1683added Aexp'.ofAexp, TotalMap.update_eq]
1684added
1685added-- Now we have quite a nice proof script: it simply identifies the Hoare rules
1686added-- that need to be used and leaves the remaining low-level details up to Lean
1687added-- to figure out.
1688added
1689added-- By now it might be apparent that the *entire* proof could be automated by a
1690added-- more ambitious tactic that also knew about the Hoare rules themselves. We
1691added-- won't build one in this chapter, so that we can get a better understanding
1692added-- of when and how the Hoare rules are used. In the next chapter, *Hoare2*,
1693added-- we'll dive deeper into automating entire proofs of Hoare triples.
1694added
1695added-- The other example of using consequence that we did earlier,
1696added-- `hoare_asgn_example2`, requires a little more work to automate. `simp`
1697added-- simplifies the assertion implication in the final bullet, but cannot finish
1698added-- it: the leftover goal is arithmetic, so it needs `lia`.
1699added
1700addedtheorem assertion_sub_example2' :
1701added {{X < 4}}
1702added X := X + 1;
1703added {{X < 5}} := by
1704added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1705added · apply hoare_asgn
1706added · simp [AssertImplies, Assertion.sub, Aexp'.ofNat, Aexp'.ofAexp,
1707added TotalMap.update_eq] -- an arithmetic goal remains
1708added lia
1709added
1710added-- Let's introduce our own tactic to handle both that bullet and the bullet
1711added-- from example 1. A `macro` declaration gives a name to a canned sequence of
1712added-- tactics:
1713added
1714added/-- Prove routine facts about assertions: unfold the Hoare-logic
1715addeddefinitions and lifting functions, simplify, and finish any leftover
1716addedarithmetic with `lia`. -/
1717addedmacro "assertion_auto" : tactic =>
1718added `(tactic| (intros
1719added <;> try (simp [AssertImplies, ValidHoareTriple, Assertion.sub,
1720added Assertion.ofProp, Aexp'.ofNat, Aexp'.ofAexp,
1721added TotalMap.update, TotalMap.getElem_def,
1722added W, X, Y, Z] at *)
1723added <;> try lia))
1724added
1725addedtheorem assertion_sub_example2'' :
1726added {{X < 4}}
1727added X := X + 1;
1728added {{X < 5}} := by
1729added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1730added · apply hoare_asgn
1731added · assertion_auto
1732added
1733addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example1''' :
1734added {{True}} X := 1; {{X = 1}} := by
1735added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1736added · apply hoare_asgn
1737added · assertion_auto
1738added
1739added-- Again, we have quite a nice proof script. All the low-level details of
1740added-- proofs about assertions have been taken care of automatically. Of course,
1741added-- `assertion_auto` isn't able to prove everything we could possibly want to
1742added-- know about assertions -- there's no magic here! But it's pretty good.
1743added
1744added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_examples_2 ⭐⭐
1745added
1746added-- Prove these triples. Try to make your proof scripts nicely automated by
1747added-- following the examples above.
1748added
1749addedtheorem assertion_sub_ex1' :
1750added {{ X ≤ 5 }}
1751added X := 2 * X;
1752added {{ X ≤ 10 }} := by
1753added all_goals
1754added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1755added · apply hoare_asgn
1756added · assertion_auto
1757added
1758addedtheorem assertion_sub_ex2' :
1759added {{ 0 ≤ 3 ∧ 3 ≤ 5 }}
1760added X := 3;
1761added {{ 0 ≤ X ∧ X ≤ 5 }} := by
1762added all_goals
1763added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1764added · apply hoare_asgn
1765added · assertion_auto
1766added
1767added-- ### Sequencing + Assignment
1768added
1769added-- Here's an example of a program involving both sequencing and assignment.
1770added-- Note the use of `hoare_seq` in conjunction with `hoare_consequence_pre` and
1771added-- `apply`'s metavariables.
1772added
1773addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example3 (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) :
1774added {{a = n}}
1775added X := ~a;
1776added skip;
1777added {{X = n}} := by
1778added apply hoare_seq
1779added · -- right part of seq
1780added apply hoare_skip
1781added · -- left part of seq
1782added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1783added · apply hoare_asgn
1784added · assertion_auto
1785added
1786added-- Informally, a nice way of displaying a proof using the sequencing rule is
1787added-- as a "decorated program" where the intermediate assertion `Q` is written
1788added-- between `c1` and `c2`:
1789added
1790added-- {{ a = n }}
1791added-- X := a
1792added-- {{ X = n }}; <--- decoration for Q
1793added-- skip
1794added-- {{ X = n }}
1795added
1796added-- We'll come back to the idea of decorated programs in much more detail in
1797added-- the next chapter.
1798added
1799added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_asgn_example4 ⭐⭐
1800added
1801added-- Translate this "decorated program" into a formal proof:
1802added
1803added-- {{ True }} ->>
1804added-- {{ 1 = 1 }}
1805added-- X := 1
1806added-- {{ X = 1 }} ->>
1807added-- {{ X = 1 ∧ 2 = 2 }};
1808added-- Y := 2
1809added-- {{ X = 1 ∧ Y = 2 }}
1810added
1811added-- Note the use of "`->>`" decorations, each marking a use of
1812added-- `hoare_consequence_pre`.
1813added
1814added-- We've started you off by providing a use of `hoare_seq` that explicitly
1815added-- identifies `X = 1` as the intermediate assertion.
1816added
1817addedtheorem hoare_asgn_example4 :
1818added {{ True }}
1819added X := 1;
1820added Y := 2;
1821added {{ X = 1 ∧ Y = 2 }} := by
1822added apply hoare_seq (Q := {{ X = 1 }})
1823added · -- right part of seq
1824added all_goals
1825added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1826added · apply hoare_asgn
1827added · assertion_auto
1828added · -- left part of seq
1829added all_goals
1830added apply hoare_consequence_pre
1831added · apply hoare_asgn
1832added · assertion_auto
1833added
1834added-- ### Exercise (3 stars): swap_exercise ⭐⭐⭐
1835added
1836added-- Write an Imp program `c` that swaps the values of `X` and `Y` and show that
1837added-- it satisfies the following specification:
1838added
1839added-- {{X ≤ Y}} c {{Y ≤ X}}
1840added
1841added-- Your proof should not need to use `unfold ValidHoareTriple`.
1842added
1843added-- Hints:
1844added
1845added-- - Remember that Imp commands need to be enclosed in `imp { … }` brackets.
1846added
1847added-- - Remember that the assignment rule works best when it's applied "back to
1848added-- front," from the postcondition to the precondition. So your proof will want
1849added-- to start at the end and work back to the beginning of your program.
1850added
1851added-- - Remember that `apply` is your friend.)
1852added
1853added-- Note to developers:
1854added-- `HIDE: CH: Here goes:
1855added-- [[
1856added-- {{ X ≤ Y }}
1857added-- Z := X
1858added-- {{ Z ≤ Y }};
1859added-- X := Y
1860added-- {{ Z ≤ X }};
1861added-- Y := Z
1862added-- {{ Y ≤ X }}
1863added-- ]]
1864added-- The _only_ catch is that one needs to do it backwards, since that's
1865added-- how the hoare_asgn rule is defined.
1866added-- Maybe move this decorated program to the decorated programs
1867added-- section, since it's a good warm-up exercise.`
1868added
1869addeddef swap_program : Com :=
1870added (imp { Z := X; X := Y; Y := Z; })
1871added
1872addedtheorem swap_exercise :
1873added {{X ≤ Y}}
1874added ~swap_program
1875added {{Y ≤ X}} := by
1876added all_goals
1877added unfold swap_program
1878added apply hoare_seq
1879added · apply hoare_seq
1880added · apply hoare_asgn
1881added · apply hoare_asgn
1882added · apply hoare_consequence_pre
1883added · apply hoare_asgn
1884added · assertion_auto
1885added
1886added-- ### Exercise (4 stars): invalid_triple (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1887added
1888added-- Show that
1889added
1890added-- {{ a = n }} X := 3; Y := a {{ Y = n }}
1891added
1892added-- is not a valid Hoare triple for some choices of `a` and `n`.
1893added
1894added-- Conceptual hint: Invent a particular `a` and `n` for which the triple in
1895added-- invalid, then use those to complete the proof.
1896added
1897added-- Technical hint: Hypothesis `h` below begins `∀ a n, ...`. You'll want to
1898added-- instantiate that with the particular `a` and `n` you've invented. You can
1899added-- do that with `have` and `apply`, but you may remember (from the
1900added-- *Automation* chapter of Logical Foundations) that Lean offers an even
1901added-- easier tactic: `specialize`. If you write
1902added
1903added-- specialize h your_a your_n
1904added
1905added-- the hypothesis will be instantiated on `your_a` and `your_n`.
1906added
1907added-- Having chosen your `a` and `n`, proceed as follows:
1908added
1909added-- - Use the (assumed) validity of the given hoare triple to derive a state
1910added-- `st'` in which `Y` has some value `y1`
1911added
1912added-- - Use the evaluation rules (`Com.EvalR.seq` and `Com.EvalR.asgn`) to show
1913added-- that `Y` has a *different* value `y2` in the same final state `st'`
1914added
1915added-- - Since `y1` and `y2` are both equal to `st'[Y]`, they are equal to each
1916added-- other. But we chose them to be different, so this is a contradiction, which
1917added-- finishes the proof.
1918added
1919addedtheorem invalid_triple : ¬ ∀ (a : Aexp) (n : Nat),
1920added {{ a = n }}
1921added X := 3; Y := ~a;
1922added {{ Y = n }} := by
1923added unfold ValidHoareTriple
1924added intro h
1925added all_goals
1926added specialize h (aexp { X }) 2 (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) (Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅)
1927added have heval : (X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) =[ X := 3; Y := X; ]=>
1928added (Y →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 3 ; X →ₜ 2 ; ∅) := by
1929added apply Com.EvalR.seq
1930added · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1931added · apply Com.EvalR.asgn; rfl
1932added apply h at heval
1933added have hcontra := heval rfl
1934added simp [Aexp'.ofAexp, Aexp'.ofNat, TotalMap.update_eq] at hcontra
1935added
1936added-- ### Conditionals
1937added
1938added-- What sort of rule do we want for reasoning about conditional commands?
1939added
1940added-- Certainly, if the same assertion `Q` holds after executing either of the
1941added-- branches, then it holds after the whole conditional. So we might be tempted
1942added-- to write:
1943added
1944added-- {{P}} c1 {{Q}}
1945added-- {{P}} c2 {{Q}}
1946added-- ---------------------------------
1947added-- {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 {{Q}}
1948added
1949added-- However, this is rather weak. For example, using this rule, we cannot show
1950added
1951added-- {{ True }}
1952added-- if X = 0
1953added-- then Y := 2
1954added-- else Y := X + 1
1955added-- end
1956added-- {{ X ≤ Y }}
1957added
1958added-- since the rule doesn't tell us enough about the state in which the
1959added-- assignments take place in the "then" and "else" branches.
1960added
1961added-- Fortunately, we can say something more precise. In the "then" branch, we
1962added-- know that the boolean expression `b` evaluates to `true`, and in the "else"
1963added-- branch, we know it evaluates to `false`. Making this information available
1964added-- in the premises of the rule gives us more information to work with when
1965added-- reasoning about the behavior of `c1` and `c2` (i.e., the reasons why they
1966added-- establish the postcondition `Q`).
1967added
1968added-- {{P ∧ b}} c1 {{Q}}
1969added-- {{P ∧ ¬ b}} c2 {{Q}}
1970added-- ------------------------------------ (hoare_if)
1971added-- {{P}} if b then c1 else c2 end {{Q}}
1972added
1973added-- To interpret this rule formally, we need to do a little work. Strictly
1974added-- speaking, the assertion we've written, `P ∧ b`, is the conjunction of an
1975added-- assertion and a boolean expression -- i.e., it doesn't typecheck. To fix
1976added-- this, we need a way of formally "lifting" any bexp `b` to an assertion.
1977added-- We'll write `bassertion b` for the assertion "the boolean expression `b`
1978added-- evaluates to `true` (in the given state)."
1979added
1980addeddef bassertion (b : Bexp) : Assertion :=
1981added fun st => (b.eval st = true)
1982added
1983added@[simp] theorem bassertion_apply (b : Bexp) (st : State) :
1984added bassertion b st = (b.eval st = true) := rfl
1985added
1986addedinstance : Coe Bexp Assertion := ⟨bassertion⟩
1987added
1988added-- A useful fact about `bassertion`:
1989added
1990added-- Note to developers (before next release):
1991added-- `Robert Rand: This isn't an identity but that's because
1992added-- we're using [~(bassertion b st)] in our triples, instead of a more
1993added-- direct/intuitive predicate.
1994added--
1995added-- Some alternatives: 1) P_True b and P_False b (defined directly as
1996added-- desired) 1) bassertion b false (adds relevant argument to bassertion)
1997added-- 2) ((bassertion (!b)) st) (clearer, but less direct).`
1998added
1999addedtheorem bexp_eval_false (b : Bexp) (st : State) (h : b.eval st = false) :
2000added ¬ ((bassertion b) st) := by
2001added simp [bassertion, h]
2002added
2003added-- Here `simp` is able to find that `b.eval st` is assumed to be `false` (by
2004added-- rewriting with `h`), notice that the goal claims it is `true`, and use the
2005added-- resulting contradiction to complete the proof.
2006added
2007added-- Note to developers (One An @meluge):
2008added-- The Rocq proof is the single tactic `congruence`. Using simp seems to
2009added-- work but should we build our own `congruence` tactic?
2010added
2011added-- Now we can formalize the Hoare proof rule for conditionals and prove it
2012added-- correct.
2013added
2014added-- The statement of the rule reads: given `htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}` and
2015added-- `hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}`, we can conclude
2016added-- `{{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}}`.
2017added
2018added-- That is (unwrapping the notations):
2019added
2020added-- theorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
2021added-- (htrue : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ bassertion b st) c1 Q)
2022added-- (hfalse : ValidHoareTriple (fun st => P st ∧ ¬ (bassertion b st)) c2 Q) :
2023added-- ValidHoareTriple P (Com.cond b c1 c2) Q
2024added
2025addedtheorem hoare_if (P Q : Assertion) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com)
2026added (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c1 {{Q}}) (hfalse : {{ P ∧ ¬b }} ~c2 {{Q}}) :
2027added {{P}} if (~b) { ~c1 } else { ~c2 } {{Q}} := by
2028added intro st st' hE hP
2029added inversion hE with
2030added | ifTrue hb hc => exact htrue _ _ hc ⟨hP, hb⟩
2031added | ifFalse hb hc => exact hfalse _ _ hc ⟨hP, bexp_eval_false b st hb⟩
2032added
2033added-- #### Example
2034added
2035added-- Here is a formal proof that the program we used to motivate the rule
2036added-- satisfies the specification we wanted.
2037added
2038addedtheorem if_example :
2039added {{True}}
2040added if (X = 0) {
2041added Y := 2;
2042added } else {
2043added Y := X + 1;
2044added }
2045added {{X ≤ Y}} := by
2046added apply hoare_if
2047added · -- Then
2048added apply hoare_consequence_pre
2049added · apply hoare_asgn
2050added · -- `assertion_auto` makes no progress here
2051added unfold AssertImplies Assertion.sub bassertion
2052added intro st ⟨_, h⟩
2053added simp only [Bexp.eval_eq, Aexp.eval_id, Aexp.eval_num, beq_iff_eq] at h
2054added simp [Aexp'.ofAexp, TotalMap.update_neq _ Y X (by decide),
2055added TotalMap.update_eq, h]
2056added · -- Else
2057added apply hoare_consequence_pre
2058added · apply hoare_asgn
2059added · assertion_auto
2060added
2061added-- As we did earlier, it would be nice to eliminate all the low-level proof
2062added-- script that isn't about the Hoare rules. Unfortunately, the
2063added-- `assertion_auto` tactic we wrote wasn't quite up to the job. Looking at the
2064added-- proof of `if_example`, we can see why: we had to unfold a definition
2065added-- (`bassertion`) that we didn't need in earlier proofs. (The step from the
2066added-- boolean equality test `st[X] == 0` to the equation `st[X] = 0` is handled
2067added-- by lemmas `simp` already knows, such as `beq_iff_eq`.) So, let's add the
2068added-- unfolding into our tactic.
2069added
2070added-- Note to developers:
2071added-- HIDE: MRC'20: There's probably a better way to engineer this. I don't
2072added-- know Ltac very well though.
2073added
2074added/-- Like `assertion_auto`, but also unfolds `bassertion`, so that facts
2075addedabout the boolean guards of conditionals and loops become available. -/
2076addedmacro "assertion_auto'" : tactic =>
2077added `(tactic| (intros
2078added <;> try (simp [AssertImplies, ValidHoareTriple, Assertion.sub,
2079added Assertion.ofProp, Aexp'.ofNat, Aexp'.ofAexp,
2080added bassertion, TotalMap.update, TotalMap.getElem_def,
2081added W, X, Y, Z] at *)
2082added <;> try lia))
2083added
2084added-- Now the proof is quite streamlined.
2085added
2086addedtheorem if_example'' :
2087added {{True}}
2088added if (X = 0) {
2089added Y := 2;
2090added } else {
2091added Y := X + 1;
2092added }
2093added {{X ≤ Y}} := by
2094added apply hoare_if
2095added · apply hoare_consequence_pre
2096added · apply hoare_asgn
2097added · assertion_auto'
2098added · apply hoare_consequence_pre
2099added · apply hoare_asgn
2100added · assertion_auto'
2101added
2102added-- We can even shorten it a little bit more.
2103added
2104addedtheorem if_example''' :
2105added {{True}}
2106added if (X = 0) {
2107added Y := 2;
2108added } else {
2109added Y := X + 1;
2110added }
2111added {{X ≤ Y}} := by
2112added apply hoare_if <;> apply hoare_consequence_pre <;>
2113added (try apply hoare_asgn) <;> try assertion_auto'
2114added
2115added-- Note to developers (Claude):
2116added-- At this point the Rocq source defines a further refinement
2117added-- `assertion_auto''` that also rewrites with `leb_le`, "for
2118added-- inequalities". In Lean the boolean comparisons produced by `Bexp.eval`
2119added-- are already reduced by `simp`'s standard `decide`/`==` lemmas, so
2120added-- `assertion_auto'` handles inequalities as it stands and no
2121added-- `assertion_auto''` is needed (nor the later `assertion_auto'''`, whose
2122added-- extra `negb`/`not_false` rewrites `simp` also covers); occurrences of
2123added-- both in the Rocq text are rendered as `assertion_auto'`.
2124added
2125added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus ⭐⭐
2126added
2127added-- Prove the theorem below using `hoare_if`. Do not use
2128added-- `unfold
2129added-- ValidHoareTriple`. The `assertion_auto'` tactic we just defined may
2130added-- be useful.
2131added
2132addedtheorem if_minus_plus :
2133added {{True}}
2134added if (X ≤ Y) {
2135added Z := Y - X;
2136added } else {
2137added Y := X + Z;
2138added }
2139added {{Y = X + Z}} := by
2140added all_goals
2141added apply hoare_if <;> apply hoare_consequence_pre <;>
2142added (try apply hoare_asgn) <;> try assertion_auto'
2143added
2144added-- #### Exercise: One-sided conditionals
2145added
2146added-- Note to developers:
2147added-- HIDE: Question from 2012, Midterm 2. One-sided conditionals.
2148added
2149added-- In this exercise we consider extending Imp with "one-sided conditionals" of
2150added-- the form `if1 (b) { c }`. Here `b` is a boolean expression, and `c` is a
2151added-- command. If `b` evaluates to `true`, then command `c` is evaluated. If `b`
2152added-- evaluates to `false`, then `if1 (b) { c }` does nothing.
2153added
2154added-- We recommend that you complete this exercise before attempting the ones
2155added-- that follow, as it should help solidify your understanding of the material.
2156added
2157added-- The first step is to extend the syntax of commands and introduce the usual
2158added-- notations. (We've done this for you, in a separate namespace to prevent
2159added-- polluting the global name space. The `scoped` notations below are active
2160added-- only inside `namespace If1`.)
2161added
2162addednamespace If1
2163added
2164addedinductive Com : Type where
2165added | skip : Com
2166added | asgn : Ident → Aexp → Com
2167added | seq : Com → Com → Com
2168added | cond : Bexp → Com → Com → Com
2169added | whileDo : Bexp → Com → Com
2170added | if1 : Bexp → Com → Com
2171added
2172added/-- If1 commands: Imp commands plus `if1` -/
2173addeddeclare_syntax_cat if1_com
2174added/-- The command that does nothing (`skip;`) -/
2175addedsyntax ident ";" : if1_com
2176added/-- Sequencing: one command after another -/
2177addedsyntax if1_com ppDedent(ppLine if1_com) : if1_com
2178added/-- Assignment -/
2179addedsyntax ident " := " imp_aexp ";" : if1_com
2180added/-- Conditional -/
2181addedsyntax "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}" ppHardSpace "else" ppHardSpace "{") ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
2182added/-- Loop -/
2183addedsyntax "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
2184added/-- One-sided conditional -/
2185addedsyntax "if1 " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : if1_com
2186added/-- Escape to Lean -/
2187addedsyntax:max "~" term:max : if1_com
2188added
2189added/-- Include an If1 command in Lean code -/
2190addedsyntax:min "imp1" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine if1_com ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
2191added
2192addedopen Lean in
2193addedmacro_rules
2194added | `(imp1 { $x:ident ; }) =>
2195added if x.getId == `skip then `(Com.skip)
2196added else Macro.throwErrorAt x s!"expected 'skip', got '{x.getId}'"
2197added | `(imp1 { $c1 $c2 }) =>
2198added `(Com.seq (imp1 {$c1}) (imp1 {$c2}))
2199added | `(imp1 { $x:ident := $a; }) =>
2200added `(Com.asgn $x (aexp {$a}))
2201added | `(imp1 { if ($b) {$c1} else {$c2} }) =>
2202added `(Com.cond (bexp {$b}) (imp1 {$c1}) (imp1 {$c2}))
2203added | `(imp1 { while ($b) {$c} }) =>
2204added `(Com.whileDo (bexp {$b}) (imp1 {$c}))
2205added | `(imp1 { if1 ($b) {$c} }) =>
2206added `(Com.if1 (bexp {$b}) (imp1 {$c}))
2207added | `(imp1 { ~$c }) =>
2208added pure c

2210added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): if1_ceval ⭐⭐
2211added
2212added-- Add two new evaluation rules to relation `Com.EvalR`, below, for `if1`. Let
2213added-- the rules for `if` guide you.
2214added
2215addedinductive Com.EvalR : Com → State → State → Prop where
2216added | skip (st : State) :
2217added EvalR (imp1 {skip;}) st st
2218added | asgn (st : State) (a : Aexp) (n : Nat) (x : Ident) (h : a.eval st = n) :
2219added EvalR (imp1 {x := ~a;}) st (x →ₜ n ; st)
2220added | seq (c1 c2 : Com) (st st' st'' : State)
2221added (h1 : EvalR c1 st st') (h2 : EvalR c2 st' st'') :
2222added EvalR (imp1 {~c1 ~c2}) st st''
2223added | ifTrue (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
2224added (hc : EvalR c1 st st') :
2225added EvalR (imp1 {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2226added | ifFalse (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c1 c2 : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false)
2227added (hc : EvalR c2 st st') :
2228added EvalR (imp1 {if (~b) {~c1} else {~c2} }) st st'
2229added | whileFalse (b : Bexp) (st : State) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
2230added EvalR (imp1 {while (~b) {~c} }) st st
2231added | whileTrue (st st' st'' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com)
2232added (hb : b.eval st = true) (hc : EvalR c st st')
2233added (hloop : EvalR (imp1 {while (~b) {~c} }) st' st'') :
2234added EvalR (imp1 {while (~b) {~c} }) st st''
2235added | if1True (st st' : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = true)
2236added (hc : EvalR c st st') :
2237added EvalR (imp1 {if1 (~b) {~c} }) st st'
2238added | if1False (st : State) (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (hb : b.eval st = false) :
2239added EvalR (imp1 {if1 (~b) {~c} }) st st
2240added

2264added-- Now we have to repeat the definition and notation of Hoare triples, so that
2265added-- they will use the updated `Com` type.
2266added
2267addeddef ValidHoareTriple
2268added (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2269added ∀ st st',
2270added (st =[ c ]=> st') →
2271added P st →
2272added Q st'
2273added
2274added/-- Hoare triple over If1 commands -/
2275addedscoped syntax:40 (priority := high)
2276added "{{" assn "}}" atomic(ppHardSpace if1_com ppHardSpace "{{") assn "}}" : term

2280added `(ValidHoareTriple ({{ $P }}) (imp1 { $c }) ({{ $Q }}))

2282added-- ### Exercise (2 stars): hoare_if1 (manually graded) ⭐⭐
2283added
2284added-- Invent a Hoare logic proof rule for `if1`. State and prove a theorem named
2285added-- `hoare_if1` that shows the validity of your rule. Use `hoare_if` as a
2286added-- guide. Try to invent a rule that is *complete*, meaning it can be used to
2287added-- prove the correctness of as many one-sided conditionals as possible. Also
2288added-- try to keep your rule *compositional*, meaning that any Imp command that
2289added-- appears in a premise should syntactically be a part of the command in the
2290added-- conclusion.
2291added
2292added-- Hint: if you encounter difficulty getting Lean to parse part of your rule
2293added-- as an assertion, try wrapping it in the `{{ … }}` brackets or adding a type
2294added-- ascription. For example, if you want `e` to be parsed as an assertion,
2295added-- write it as `(e : Assertion)`.
2296added
2297addedtheorem hoare_if1 (b : Bexp) (c : Com) (P Q : Assertion)
2298added (htrue : {{ P ∧ b }} ~c {{ Q }})
2299added (hfalse : ({{ P ∧ ¬b }}) ->> Q) :
2300added {{ P }} if1 (~b) { ~c } {{ Q }} := by
2301added intro st st' heval hpre
2302added inversion heval with
2303added | if1True hb hc => exact htrue _ _ hc ⟨hpre, hb⟩
2304added | if1False hb => exact hfalse _ ⟨hpre, bexp_eval_false b st hb⟩
2305added
2306added-- For example (`hoare_if1_good`) your rule should be strong enough to show
2307added-- the following Hoare triple is valid:
2308added
2309added-- {{ X + Y = Z }}
2310added-- if1 (Y ≠ 0) {
2311added-- X := X + Y;
2312added-- }
2313added-- {{ X = Z }}
2314added
2315added-- Before the next exercise, we need to restate the Hoare rules of consequence
2316added-- (for preconditions) and assignment for the new `Com` type.
2317added
2318addedtheorem hoare_consequence_pre (P P' Q : Assertion) (c : Com)
2319added (hhoare : {{P'}} ~c {{Q}}) (himp : P ->> P') :
2320added {{P}} ~c {{Q}} := by
2321added intro st st' heval hpre
2322added exact hhoare st st' heval (himp st hpre)
2323added
2324addedtheorem hoare_asgn (Q : Assertion) (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) :
2325added {{Q [x ↦ ~a]}} x := ~a; {{Q}} := by
2326added intro st st' heval hQ
2327added inversion heval with
2328added | asgn n h =>
2329added subst h
2330added exact hQ
2331added

2335added

2349addedtheorem hoare_if1_good :
2350added {{ X + Y = Z }}

2355added all_goals
